svg.title: The whole install, from an empty project to a locked-down GitLab: One interactive install builds the framework and configures GitLab
svg.text: The whole install, from an empty project to a locked-down
Scenario: One interactive install builds the framework and configures GitLab

g.text: Given a brand-new empty project waits on GitLab
GitLab's home page of a brand-new project, as its owner sees it. GitLab says "The repository for this project is empty"
and lists the commands that push a first commit.
The project's random name shows as "project", and dates and avatars are hidden, so the picture is the same on every run.
When the developer starts the toolbox installer in the freshly cloned
project
The developer's terminal, in the clone of that empty project. Git answers "No commits yet",
then the installer starts and asks its first question, "Install the complete DevSecOps
framework?".
The card lists the two choices, "Complete framework" and "Choose components". The highlighted
button, "Install everything", is the default answer and takes the complete framework.
And the developer answers the eleven setup questions, keeping every
default
Saying yes to the complete framework opens the eleven setup questions of Copier, the tool
that builds the project from the answers. The developer presses Enter on each one and keeps
its default.
The card is caught on the last question, the language of the test descriptions, with its
default "en". Above it, the ten answers already given: No to Ansible, GitLab SaaS
(gitlab.com), the runner tag saas-linux-medium-amd64, Docker, then Yes, Yes, Yes, No, Yes and
Yes.
Then the installer prints only the merge request settings it gave
GitLab, never the project's runner token
On the way, the installer sets the project's merge request rules on GitLab. This part
scrolled by: "Applying merge request settings...", one line per setting GitLab now holds,
such as "merge_method = ff", and "GitLab merge request settings configured".
GitLab answers that change with the whole project, its runner registration token included: a
secret that lets a machine sign up to run the project's jobs. The test reads that token from
GitLab and checks that the whole session never printed it.
The test also runs the same step with a merge method GitLab refuses. The step fails on
GitLab's own reason, and prints no token either.
Then the installer's merge request into the main branch now waits for review on GitLab
The installer builds the framework, pushes it to a new branch, init-framework-devsecops, and opens a merge request into
the main branch. This is GitLab's page for it: "chore: initialize devsecops framework", Open.
A merge request is a change that waits for review before it joins the main branch. The framework never reaches the main
branch any other way.
Then GitLab now lets the main branch accept only fast-forward merges
The project's merge request settings. "Fast-forward merge" is selected, so the history of the main branch stays a
straight line.
Under "Merge checks", "Pipelines must succeed" and "All threads must be resolved" are ticked: nothing broken or still
under discussion can merge.
And GitLab now refuses pushes straight to the main branch
The protected branches settings. On the main branch, "Allowed to merge" is "Maintainers" and "Allowed to push and merge"
is "No one": every change has to go through a merge request.
And GitLab now holds the project's two automation tokens
The project access tokens page lists the two tokens the install created: TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN, which the release uses,
and TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN, which the update bot uses. Both have the Maintainer role.
And GitLab now keeps both tokens as CI/CD variables
The project's CI/CD variables hold both tokens under the same names, so the pipeline can read them. GitLab shows their
values as dots.
And GitLab now runs Renovate from a nightly pipeline schedule
The project's pipeline schedules. The install created one, "Renovate", on the main branch, once a night between 2 and 5
am, Paris time. The hour and the minute come from the project's number, so the projects of a group do not all start at
once.
Pipelines on the main branch now leave Renovate to this schedule, so a merge no longer rebases every open Renovate merge
request.
Then the framework's first pipeline passes, its MegaLinter job green on every linter, the
secret and dependency scanners included
A runner, the machine that runs pipelines, now serves this project, and the merge request's pipeline runs every job the
framework ships. All of them pass.
The card is the log of one of them, the code:megalinter job: MegaLinter's verdict for each of its linters, one line
each, every one "successfully". The secret and dependency scanners betterleaks, grype, trivy and trufflehog are among
them.
The panel on the right says the job and its pipeline Passed, and lists the other code jobs of the pipeline, all green.
And the merge request merges into the main branch
The same merge request page as in chapter 1, now Merged. "Merge request pipeline passed" shows its stages, all green, as
the "Pipelines must succeed" rule demands, and "Deleted the source branch" closes the review.
Below it, "Pipeline passed on main": the merge started the main branch's own pipeline, and its three stages, plan,
release and feedback, passed too. With only chores in the history, the release makes no new version, and the job still
passes.
And the main branch now carries the whole framework, merged through review
The same home page as the first card. The main branch now holds the whole framework, .agents, .claude, .config,
.gitlab-ci.yml and Taskfile.yml among them, on the commit "chore: initialize devsecops framework". Only README.md stays
on "chore: initialize repository", the commit the installer made to create the main branch. The green check next to the
last commit is the main branch's pipeline, passed.
The first install is proven end to end.

svg.text: Storyboard e2e · 13 steps · 13 frames · every frame is its own pixel baseline (tolerance: 0)
● Given: stage ● When: actions ● Then: proofs
